opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot. The biggest one is credit assignment over long horizons. Most of the RL we do with language models today is outcome-based: you sample a trajectory, check whether the final answer is right, and push that one scalar reward back over thousands of tokens. That works surprisingly well when episodes are short and the reward is crisp, like a math problem with a verifiable answer or a unit test that passes or fails. But it's very sample-inefficient. The model doesn't really learn which of the hundred decisions it made actually mattered. As we move toward agents that run for hours, write and refactor whole codebases, and take many actions in an environment, that problem gets much worse. A sparse signal at the end of a very long episode just isn't enough.

The second weakness is reward specification. RL is only as good as the signal you're optimizing, and outside of verifiable domains we don't have great reward functions. Learned reward models get exploited. The policy finds the seams, and you get reward hacking: outputs that look good to the grader but aren't actually good. So a lot of the art right now is building environments and graders that are robust enough to optimize against hard. That's more of a craft than a science today, and it doesn't scale cleanly.

Third is exploration. In classic deep RL, AlphaGo and so on, exploration was a central research problem. With language models we've sidestepped it by starting from a strong pretrained prior, so the model already proposes reasonable things. But that also means we mostly sharpen behaviors the model could already do some fraction of the time. Whether current methods can discover genuinely new strategies, rather than amplifying ones already latent in the base model, is an open question. I think real, directed exploration is going to matter a lot more as we push into tasks where the prior isn't good enough.

And finally there's generalization and continual learning. We train on a distribution of environments and hope the skills transfer. Sometimes they do, impressively. But we don't have a principled understanding of why RL on one set of tasks generalizes to another. The systems also don't keep learning from experience after deployment the way a person on the job does. Closing that loop, so an agent gets better from its own interactions in a stable way, is one of the most important unsolved pieces.

So to summarize: long-horizon credit assignment, robust rewards beyond verifiable domains, exploration, and continual learning. Those are where I'd expect the most algorithmic progress over the next few years.

r002.rationale: It describes the difficulty of assigning credit over long episodes, but does not attribute meandering reasoning chains to a lack of step-level credit assignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the core RL algorithms themselves are actually in pretty good shape. If you look at something like PPO or the policy gradient family, those have been around for a while and they work. The weaknesses are less about the update rule and more about everything around it.

The first big one is sample efficiency. RL is incredibly data hungry. You need an enormous number of environment interactions to learn anything, and that's fine in a simulator where you can run millions of episodes, but it becomes a real bottleneck the moment the environment is expensive, like a real robot or a real user. A lot of what made RL work in language models is that we found a way to get a very dense, cheap signal, but that doesn't generalize to every domain.

The second is exploration. Most methods still rely on fairly naive exploration, essentially adding noise and hoping you stumble onto something good. For short-horizon tasks that's okay. For long-horizon tasks, where you need a sequence of many correct steps before you see any reward, the probability of randomly finding the good trajectory collapses exponentially. We don't have a great principled answer for that yet. Humans explore very differently. We form hypotheses, we have curiosity, we reason about what might work before trying it.

The third, and this is maybe the one I think about most, is credit assignment and reward design. The algorithm is only as good as the signal you give it. In a lot of real problems you have a sparse outcome reward at the end, and figuring out which of the hundred decisions along the way actually mattered is hard. And if you try to fix that by hand-designing dense rewards, you get reward hacking, where the agent optimizes exactly what you wrote rather than what you meant. So the research frontier has shifted toward learned reward models, verifiers, and ways of getting good supervision at scale, because that's where the real leverage is.

And then there's generalization. Classic RL agents are superhuman in the narrow environment they trained in and fall apart the moment anything changes. The exciting thing about combining RL with large pretrained models is that the model brings priors and world knowledge, so you're not learning from scratch anymore. That doesn't fix the algorithmic issues, but it changes which ones matter. You care much less about learning from nothing and much more about scaling the feedback loop reliably.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest weakness is how inefficiently we use experience. In a typical reinforcement learning setup, you generate a lot of attempts, score them, and then use those scores to update the policy. But a failed attempt can contain a tremendous amount of information. A scalar reward doesn’t necessarily tell you which decision was wrong, why it was wrong, or what you should do differently.

That becomes particularly challenging over long horizons. If an agent takes a hundred actions and fails at the end, how do you assign credit? Was the problem the last action, or a bad assumption it made at the beginning? And exploration is coupled to that: if the model almost never discovers a successful trajectory, there’s very little signal to reinforce.

Language models give us an interesting opportunity here because they already have a lot of knowledge and can express intermediate reasoning. The question is how to turn that into a better learning algorithm—one that can extract useful lessons from failures, explore deliberately, and retain what it learns across tasks. Getting a higher reward on a particular task is one thing. Learning something that makes the next task easier is the more fundamental challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest weakness is that reinforcement learning still asks you to discover too much through trial and error. You start with a policy, it generates some experience, you get a reward signal, and then you try to figure out which decisions were responsible for that reward. If the task is long and the reward is sparse, that’s a very inefficient way to learn.

There are two problems tangled up in that. One is exploration: how do you find a successful trajectory in the first place? The other is credit assignment: once you find it, how do you extract the right lesson? A system can fail at either one, and simply collecting more rollouts can be an expensive way to compensate.

The other weakness is how little experience we reuse. Humans can watch someone do something, read an explanation, or make a mistake once and carry that knowledge into a different setting. Traditional RL systems tend to be much more specialized. They learn a policy for a particular environment, and a lot of that learning doesn’t transfer.

Pretrained models give us a much better starting point because they already contain useful knowledge and behaviors. But that changes the algorithmic question: how do you use reinforcement learning to reliably improve those capabilities, especially on tasks that require many steps, without spending an enormous amount of computation getting a very small amount of useful feedback? I think that’s where a lot of the interesting work is.
